questions.stem: An application must encrypt 50 MB files with a key that is protected by AWS KMS. Which combination of steps should the developer take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send each file to the KMS Encrypt API and store the ciphertext that it returns
options.rationale: Encrypt accepts only small amounts of data, so it cannot encrypt large files directly.

options.text: Store the encrypted data key with the file and erase the plaintext key
options.rationale: Only AWS KMS can decrypt the stored data key, so access to the file stays under the KMS key.

options.text: Export the KMS key and encrypt the files with it directly
options.rationale: KMS keys do not leave AWS KMS unencrypted.

options.text: Call GenerateDataKey and encrypt each file locally with the plaintext key
options.rationale: GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext and an encrypted copy of a data key; the plaintext copy encrypts the data outside KMS.

options.text: Store the plaintext data key next to each file so the file can be decrypted later
options.rationale: Anyone with the file could then decrypt it.

questions.explanation: Envelope encryption: a data key from GenerateDataKey encrypts large data locally, and only the KMS-encrypted copy of that key is kept with the data. Calling Encrypt directly is the trap, because it accepts only small payloads.

questions.stem: Objects in an Amazon S3 bucket must be encrypted at rest with a key whose use is controlled by a key policy and logged in AWS CloudTrail. Which encryption option meets these requirements?

options.text: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
options.rationale: S3 manages these keys for you, so there is no key policy to control.

options.text: Server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)
options.rationale: With SSE-C you manage the keys yourself outside AWS KMS.

options.text: No encryption, with a bucket policy that denies public access
options.rationale: Blocking public access is not encryption at rest.

options.text: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)
options.rationale: SSE-KMS uses a KMS key with its own policy, and each use of it is logged in CloudTrail.

questions.explanation: Choose SSE-KMS when you need control over who can use the key and an audit trail of its use.

questions.stem: A company requires that data is encrypted before it leaves the application, so that AWS never receives it in plaintext. Which approach meets this requirement?

options.text: Client-side encryption, for example with the AWS Encryption SDK
options.rationale: Data is encrypted in the application before it is sent to AWS.

options.text: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys
options.rationale: S3 receives the plaintext and encrypts it on arrival.

options.text: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys that the company manages
options.rationale: S3 still receives the plaintext before encrypting it.

options.text: HTTPS between the application and AWS
options.rationale: TLS protects data in transit but AWS decrypts it on arrival.

questions.explanation: Server-side encryption protects data at rest after AWS receives it; client-side encryption protects it before it is sent.

questions.stem: A security review requires that all requests to an Amazon S3 bucket use HTTPS. What should the developer add?

options.text: Default bucket encryption with SSE-S3 applied to every object that is uploaded
options.rationale: Default encryption protects data at rest, not in transit.

options.text: A bucket policy that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false
options.rationale: The condition blocks any request made over plain HTTP.

options.text: S3 Versioning
options.rationale: Versioning keeps object versions and has nothing to do with transport.

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle rule
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules move and delete objects by age.

questions.explanation: The aws:SecureTransport condition key is the standard way to require TLS for a bucket.

questions.stem: An Application Load Balancer needs a public TLS certificate for www.example.com that renews automatically. What should the developer use?

options.text: A self-signed certificate imported into ACM and attached to the listener
options.rationale: Browsers do not trust self-signed certificates, and imported ones are not renewed by ACM.

options.text: A certificate from AWS Private CA
options.rationale: Private certificates are trusted only inside your organization, not by public browsers.

options.text: A public ACM certificate attached to the HTTPS listener
options.rationale: ACM issues public certificates and manages their renewal, automatically when DNS validation is used.

options.text: An Amazon EC2 key pair
options.rationale: Key pairs are for SSH access, not TLS.

questions.explanation: The clues are a public certificate and automatic renewal, which a public ACM certificate on the listener provides. AWS Private CA is the nearest distractor, but browsers do not trust private certificates.

questions.stem: A developer requested an ACM certificate in the eu-west-1 Region, but it does not appear when configuring a custom domain for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. What should the developer do?

options.text: Add the eu-west-1 certificate's ARN to the distribution's origin settings
options.rationale: Origin settings describe where CloudFront fetches content; the viewer certificate must come from ACM in us-east-1.

options.text: Wait for the certificate to replicate to all Regions
options.rationale: ACM certificates are Regional and do not replicate.

options.text: Upload the certificate to the S3 origin bucket
options.rationale: Origins do not supply certificates for the distribution's domain.

options.text: Request or import the certificate in the US East (N. Virginia) Region
options.rationale: CloudFront uses certificates from ACM in us-east-1.

questions.explanation: Certificates for CloudFront must be in us-east-1, whatever Region the origin is in.

questions.stem: Internal microservices must use TLS certificates issued by the company's own certificate authority. The certificates do not need to be trusted by public browsers. Which service should the developer use?

options.text: AWS Private CA
options.rationale: Private CA issues private certificates for internal services and devices.

options.text: Public certificates from AWS Certificate Manager
options.rationale: Public certificates are for publicly trusted domains.

options.text: AWS Secrets Manager
options.rationale: Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets; it does not issue certificates.

options.text: AWS KMS asymmetric keys
options.rationale: KMS keys sign and encrypt data but are not a certificate authority.

questions.explanation: Use AWS Private CA for an internal PKI; use public ACM certificates for public endpoints.

questions.stem: A developer needs an SSH key pair to connect to a new development instance. The developer wants AWS to keep only the public key. What should the developer do?

options.text: Create an asymmetric key in AWS KMS and download its private key
options.rationale: KMS never exports the private key of an asymmetric KMS key.

options.text: Create an EC2 key pair and download its private key once
options.rationale: EC2 stores the public key and gives you the private key once.

options.text: Request a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager
options.rationale: ACM certificates are for TLS, not SSH sign-in.

options.text: Store a password in AWS Secrets Manager
options.rationale: A password is not an SSH key pair.

questions.explanation: EC2 key pairs (created in EC2 or imported) are the standard way to get SSH keys for instances.

questions.stem: Application logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs sometimes contain email addresses and credit card numbers. Most people who read the logs must not see these values. What should the developer configure?

options.text: AWS KMS encryption of the log group with a customer managed key that rotates
options.rationale: Encryption protects data at rest, but anyone allowed to read the logs still sees the values.

options.text: A shorter retention period
options.rationale: Shorter retention limits how long data is kept, not who sees it.

options.text: A data protection policy on the log group that masks sensitive data
options.rationale: Matching data is masked when the logs are viewed unless the reader has unmask permission.

options.text: A metric filter that counts the sensitive values
options.rationale: Metric filters create metrics; they do not hide log content.

questions.explanation: The clue is that most readers must not see the values: a data protection policy masks them for anyone without unmask permission. Encryption is the trap, because it protects stored data but not what an allowed reader sees.

questions.stem: A Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database. The password must not appear in code or configuration and must rotate automatically. Which steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Package the password in a Lambda layer
options.rationale: The secret would sit in plaintext in every function that uses the layer.

options.text: Allow the execution role to read the secret, and fetch it at runtime
options.rationale: With secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, the function fetches the current password when it needs it.

options.text: Store the password as a String parameter in Parameter Store
options.rationale: A plain String parameter is not encrypted and does not rotate.

options.text: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation
options.rationale: Secrets Manager rotates database credentials on a schedule.

options.text: Store the password in an environment variable and redeploy to rotate it
options.rationale: The password is visible in the configuration and rotation is manual.

questions.explanation: Secrets Manager plus a runtime lookup keeps secrets out of code and supports rotation; caching the value reduces calls.

questions.stem: A role in account B must decrypt data with a customer managed AWS KMS key that belongs to account A. Calls from account B currently fail with AccessDenied. Which combination of steps will allow the decryption? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Update the key policy in account A to allow account B to use the key for kms:Decrypt
options.rationale: A key used across accounts must be allowed by its key policy.

options.text: Create a grant in account B on its own copy of the key
options.rationale: Account B has no copy of the key; the key and its policy live in account A.

options.text: Use an AWS managed key, which can be shared with other accounts
options.rationale: AWS managed keys cannot be used across accounts; their policies cannot be changed.

options.text: Give the role in account B an IAM policy that allows kms:Decrypt on the key's ARN
options.rationale: Account B must also delegate the permission to its role with an IAM policy.

options.text: Enable automatic key rotation on the key in account A
options.rationale: Rotation changes key material on a schedule; it does not grant access.

questions.explanation: Cross-account KMS use needs both the key policy in the owning account and an IAM policy in the calling account.

questions.stem: An application needs a software license key at startup. The value must be stored encrypted, it never changes, and the team wants the lowest-cost option. Where should the developer store it?

options.text: An AWS Secrets Manager secret, encrypted with the default key
options.rationale: Secrets Manager suits credentials that need rotation and charges per secret, so it is not the lowest-cost choice for a value that never changes.

options.text: A plaintext environment variable in the application's configuration
options.rationale: Anyone who can read the configuration sees the value in plaintext.

options.text: Store it as a SecureString parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
options.rationale: SecureString parameters are encrypted with AWS KMS, and the standard parameter tier has no additional charge.

options.text: A String parameter in Parameter Store, encrypted by the application
options.rationale: This adds custom encryption code when SecureString already handles encryption.

questions.explanation: For an encrypted configuration value such as a license key, a Parameter Store SecureString is the simple, low-cost choice. AWS recommends Secrets Manager for credentials such as passwords and API keys.

questions.stem: A multi-tenant application encrypts each tenant's records with one AWS KMS key. Data encrypted for one tenant must fail to decrypt if it is presented as another tenant's data, and the tenant ID should appear in AWS CloudTrail logs of key use. What should the developer use?

options.text: A separate KMS key alias for each tenant, each pointing to the same underlying key
options.rationale: Aliases are names; data encrypted through one alias decrypts through any alias for that key.

options.text: Automatic key rotation, with the tenant ID used as the rotation period
options.rationale: Rotation is a schedule for new key material and has no notion of tenants.

options.text: A tag on the KMS key with every tenant's ID as the tag value
options.rationale: Key tags describe the key; they are not bound to individual ciphertexts.

options.text: An encryption context with the tenant ID on each encrypt and decrypt call
options.rationale: The encryption context is bound to the ciphertext, must match on decrypt, and is recorded in CloudTrail.

questions.explanation: Encryption context is additional authenticated data that ties ciphertext to its context and shows up in audit logs.

questions.stem: A busy Lambda function calls GetSecretValue on every invocation to read a database password from AWS Secrets Manager. This adds latency and cost. The password rotates monthly. What should the developer do?

options.text: Cache the secret with the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension
options.rationale: Caching the value with a refresh interval avoids a call on every invocation while still picking up rotated values.

options.text: Copy the password into an environment variable each time the function is deployed
options.rationale: The function would keep the old password after the monthly rotation.

options.text: Increase the function's memory so that GetSecretValue returns faster
options.rationale: Memory does not remove the per-invocation API call or its cost.

options.text: Read the secret once per day with a scheduled EventBridge rule
options.rationale: A scheduled rule cannot hand the value to running function environments.

questions.explanation: Cache secrets in the execution environment, with a refresh so that rotated values are picked up.

questions.stem: A security policy requires that every connection from an application to its Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database is encrypted in transit. Unencrypted connections must be refused. What should the developer do?

options.text: Enable encryption at rest on the database instance with an AWS KMS key
options.rationale: Encryption at rest protects stored data, not connections.

options.text: Set rds.force_ssl to 1 in the parameter group and connect over SSL/TLS
options.rationale: The parameter makes the database reject connections that do not use SSL/TLS.

options.text: Place the database in a private subnet with a restrictive security group
options.rationale: Network isolation limits who can connect but does not encrypt the connection.

options.text: Store the database password in AWS Secrets Manager with rotation
options.rationale: Protecting the password does not encrypt traffic.

questions.explanation: Encryption in transit to RDS is enforced in the database's parameters; clients connect with SSL/TLS.

questions.stem: An Amazon S3 bucket uses SSE-KMS by default. An application writes millions of small objects, and the AWS KMS request charges are high. What should the developer enable to reduce them?

options.text: Automatic rotation of the KMS key used by the bucket
options.rationale: Rotation changes key material; it does not reduce KMS requests.

options.text: Client-side encryption with a new data key for every object
options.rationale: A new data key per object still needs a KMS request per object.

options.text: Turn on S3 Bucket Keys for the bucket's SSE-KMS encryption
options.rationale: A bucket-level key cuts the number of requests that S3 makes to AWS KMS.

options.text: S3 Versioning on the bucket, so objects are encrypted once
options.rationale: Versioning keeps object versions and has no effect on KMS requests.

questions.explanation: S3 Bucket Keys reduce request traffic from S3 to AWS KMS for SSE-KMS.

questions.stem: A log group has a data protection policy that masks email addresses and credit card numbers. Developers must keep seeing masked values, but the security team must be able to see the original values during investigations. What should the developer do?

options.text: Remove the data protection policy whenever an investigation starts
options.rationale: This unmasks the data for everyone who can read the log group.

options.text: Copy the log group to an unencrypted S3 bucket for the security team
options.rationale: Copying sensitive logs widens exposure and does not use the masking controls.

options.text: Give the security team logs:GetLogEvents on the log group
options.rationale: Reading events still returns masked values without the unmask permission.

options.text: Grant the logs:Unmask permission to the security team's role
options.rationale: Users with logs:Unmask can view the unmasked data; everyone else sees masked values.

questions.explanation: CloudWatch Logs data protection masks sensitive data, and the logs:Unmask permission controls who can see the originals.

questions.stem: Compliance rules require that a customer managed AWS KMS key gets new key material every year. Data encrypted under the old key material must still decrypt, and the application must not change. What should the developer do?

options.text: Enable automatic key rotation on the customer managed KMS key, yearly
options.rationale: KMS keeps the old key material for decryption and uses the new material for new encryption, under the same key ID.

options.text: Create a new key every year and re-encrypt the existing data by hand
options.rationale: This works but changes the key the application uses and adds manual work.

options.text: Delete the key every year so that AWS KMS creates a replacement
options.rationale: Deleting the key makes data encrypted with it unrecoverable.

options.text: Change the key's alias to point to a new key every year
options.rationale: The alias change alone breaks decryption of older data unless the old key is also kept.

questions.explanation: Automatic rotation of a customer managed key is transparent to applications.

questions.stem: A developer requested a public certificate in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) with DNS validation for api.example.com. The domain is hosted in Amazon Route 53. The certificate has stayed in Pending validation status. What should the developer do?

options.text: Import the certificate into ACM again with a new private key
options.rationale: Importing does not validate a requested certificate and is a different workflow.

options.text: Add the CNAME record that ACM provides to the hosted zone
options.rationale: ACM validates domain control by finding that CNAME record; it can be created from the ACM console.

options.text: Wait for the validation email and click the approval link in it
options.rationale: That applies to email validation, not DNS validation.

options.text: Attach the certificate to a load balancer to finish validation
options.rationale: A certificate cannot be used before it is issued.

questions.explanation: DNS validation needs the CNAME record that ACM supplies to exist in the domain's DNS.

questions.stem: An application stores a third-party API key in AWS Secrets Manager. The key must change every 30 days without downtime, and the third party offers an API to issue new keys. Which combination of steps will meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Copy the key into an environment variable every 30 days
options.rationale: Manual copying does not rotate the key at the provider and risks downtime.

options.text: Write a rotation Lambda function that creates, sets, tests and finishes the new key
options.rationale: For a third-party key, a custom rotation function calls the provider's API in the rotation steps.

options.text: Move the key to a Parameter Store SecureString with rotation turned on
options.rationale: Parameter Store does not rotate parameter values.

options.text: Turn on rotation for the secret with a 30-day schedule
options.rationale: Secrets Manager runs rotation on the schedule and stores each new version.

options.text: Enable automatic rotation on the KMS key that encrypts the secret
options.rationale: Rotating the KMS key changes the encryption key, not the API key stored in the secret.

questions.explanation: Secrets Manager rotation uses a Lambda function; for non-database secrets, the function implements the provider's steps.

questions.stem: A company must manage its own encryption keys outside AWS, but it wants Amazon S3 to perform the encryption and decryption of objects. Which option should the developer use?

options.text: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
options.rationale: With SSE-S3, AWS manages the keys.

options.text: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)
options.rationale: The keys are in AWS KMS, not managed by the company outside AWS.

options.text: Server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)
options.rationale: With SSE-C, the client sends its own key with each request, and S3 encrypts or decrypts without storing the key.

options.text: Client-side encryption done before each upload
options.rationale: This keeps keys outside AWS, but S3 would not perform the encryption.

questions.explanation: SSE-C: the customer manages the keys, and S3 encrypts with the key supplied in each request, without storing it. Since April 2026, SSE-C is blocked by default on new general purpose buckets, so it must be allowed in the bucket's encryption settings first.

questions.stem: A new DynamoDB table must be encrypted at rest with a key whose key policy the company controls and whose use is logged in AWS CloudTrail. What should the developer choose when creating the table?

options.text: The default AWS owned key for encryption at rest
options.rationale: AWS owned keys are not in the company's account, and their policies cannot be changed.

options.text: Client-side encryption of every attribute in the application
options.rationale: This adds custom code and is not the table's encryption-at-rest setting.

options.text: Turning off encryption so that a key can be added later
options.rationale: DynamoDB always encrypts data at rest; it cannot be turned off.

options.text: A customer managed AWS KMS key for the table's encryption
options.rationale: A customer managed key has a key policy the company controls, and its use is recorded in CloudTrail.

questions.explanation: DynamoDB encrypts all tables at rest; a customer managed key adds control and auditing.

questions.stem: A company requires that every new Amazon EBS volume in an account and Region is encrypted, even when a developer forgets to choose encryption. What should the developer turn on?

options.text: EBS encryption by default for the account in that Region
options.rationale: With encryption by default, new volumes and snapshot copies are encrypted automatically.

options.text: Automatic rotation on the KMS key used for EBS
options.rationale: Rotation changes key material; it does not make unencrypted volumes encrypted.

options.text: Encryption on each EC2 instance's root volume by hand
options.rationale: Manual steps are what the requirement wants to avoid.

options.text: An S3 bucket policy that requires the aws:SecureTransport condition
options.rationale: That applies to S3 requests, not to EBS volumes.

questions.explanation: EBS encryption by default is a per-Region account setting.
